L1@P0: A Second-Order Unsplit Godunov Scheme for Cell-Centered MHD: the
L2@P0: CTU-GLM scheme.
L3@P0: Andrea Mignone∗,a, Petros Tzeferacosa
L4@P0: aDipartimento di Fisica Generale, Universit´a degli studi di Torino
L5@P0: Abstract
L6@P0: We assess the validity of a single step Godunov scheme for the solution of the magneto-hydrodynamics
L7@P0: equations in more than one dimension. The scheme is second-order accurate and the temporal discretization
L8@P0: is based on the dimensionally unsplit Corner Transport Upwind (CTU) method of Colella. The proposed
L9@P0: scheme employs a cell-centered representation of the primary fluid variables (including magnetic field) and
L10@P0: conserves mass, momentum, magnetic induction and energy. A variant of the scheme, which breaks momentum and energy conservation, is also considered. Divergence errors are transported out of the domain and
L11@P0: damped using the mixed hyperbolic/parabolic divergence cleaning technique by Dedner et al. (J. Comput.
L12@P0: Phys., 175, 2002). The strength and accuracy of the scheme are verified by a direct comparison with the eightwave formulation (also employing a cell-centered representation) and with the popular constrained transport
L13@P0: method, where magnetic field components retain a staggered collocation inside the computational cell. Results obtained from two- and three-dimensional test problems indicate that the newly proposed scheme is
L14@P0: robust, accurate and competitive with recent implementations of the constrained transport method while
L15@P0: being considerably easier to implement in existing hydro codes.
L16@P0: Key words: Magnetohydrodynamics, Compressible Flow, Unsplit scheme, High-order Godunov method,
L17@P0: Cell-centered method
L18@P0: 1. Introduction
L19@P0: A primary aspect in building stable and robust Godunov type schemes for the numerical solution of the
L20@P0: compressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations relies on an accurate way to control the solenoidal
L21@P0: property of the magnetic field while preserving the conservation properties of the underlying physical laws.
L22@P0: Failure to fulfill either requisite has been reported as a potential hassle leading to unphysical effects such
L23@P0: as plasma acceleration in the direction of the field, incorrect jump conditions, wrong propagation speed of
L24@P0: discontinuities and odd-even decoupling, see [26, 4]. A comprehensive body of literature has been dedicated
L25@P0: to this subject and several strategies to enforce the ∇ · B = 0 condition in Godunov-type codes have been
L26@P0: proposed, see for example [28, 24, 25, 2, 26] and, more recently, [3, 18, 15, 23, 19]. The robustness of one
L27@P0: method over another can be established on a practical base by extensive numerical testing, see [26, 4].
L28@P0: In a first class of schemes, the magnetic field is discretized as a cell-centered quantity and the usual formalism already developed for the Euler equation can be extended in a natural way. Cell-centered methods
L29@P0: are appealing since the extensions to adaptive and/or unstructured grids are of straightforward implementation. Moreover, the same interpolation scheme and stencil used for the other hydrodynamic variables can be
L30@P0: easily adapted since all quantities are discretized at the same spatial location, thus facilitating the extension
L31@P0: to schemes possessing higher than second order accuracy. Unfortunately, numerical methods based on a
L32@P0: cell-centered discretization do not naturally preserve Gauss’s law of electromagnetism, even if ∇ · B = 0

L35@P0-1: Preprint submitted to Journal of Computational Physics June 15, 2021initially. In the approach suggested by Powell [21, 22], Gauss’s law for magnetism is discarded in the derivation of the MHD equations and the resulting system of hyperbolic laws is no longer conservative by the
L36@P1: appearance of a source term proportional to ∇ · B. Although the source term should be physically zero at
L37@P1: the continuous level, Powell showed that its inclusion changes the character of the equations by introducing
L38@P1: an additional eighth wave corresponding to the propagation of jumps in the component of magnetic field
L39@P1: normal to a given interface. A different approach is followed in the projection scheme [6, 28, 24, 9], where a
L40@P1: Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition is applied to resolve B as the sum of an irrotational and a solenoidal part,
L41@P1: associated with scalar and vector potentials. A cleaning step allows to recover the divergence-free magnetic
L42@P1: field by subtracting the unphysical contribution coming from the irrotational component at the extra cost of
L43@P1: solving a Poisson equation. In the approach of Dedner et al. [12], the divergence-free constraint is enforced
L44@P1: by solving a modified system of conservation laws where the induction equation is coupled to a generalized
L45@P1: Lagrange multiplier. Dedner et al. showed that the choice of mixed hyperbolic/parabolic correction offers
L46@P1: both propagation and dissipation of divergence errors with the maximal admissible characteristic speed,
L47@P1: independently of the fluid velocity. This approach preserves the full conservation form of the original MHD
L48@P1: system at the minimal cost of introducing one additional variable in the system and will be our scheme of
L49@P1: choice. Finally, Torrilhon [27] (see also [1]) showed a general procedure to modify the inter-cell fluxes in the
L50@P1: framework of a flux distribution scheme that preserves the value of a certain discrete divergence operator in
L51@P1: each control volume.
L52@P1: A different strategy is followed in the constrained transport (CT) methods, originally devised by [13]
L53@P1: and later built into the framework of shock-capturing Godunov methods by a number of investigators, e.g.,
L54@P1: [2, 3, 18, 15, 16]. In this class of schemes, the magnetic field has a staggered representation whereby the
L55@P1: different components live on the face they are normal to. Hydrodynamic variables (density, velocity and
L56@P1: pressure) retains their usual collocation at the cell center. CT schemes preserve the divergence-free condition
L57@P1: to machine accuracy in an integral sense since the magnetic field is treated as a surface averaged quantity and
L58@P1: thus more naturally updated using Stokes’ theorem. This evolutionary step involves the construction of a
L59@P1: line-averaged electric field along the face edges, thereby requiring some sort of reconstruction or averaging of
L60@P1: the electromotive force from the face center (where different components are usually available as face centered
L61@P1: upwind Godunov fluxes) to the edges. A variety of different strategies have been suggested, including simple
L62@P1: arithmetic averaging [2, 25], solution of 2-D Riemann problems [18, 14] or other somewhat more empirical
L63@P1: approaches [15, 16, 17]. The staggered collocation of magnetic and electric field variables in CT schemes
L64@P1: makes their extension to adaptive grids rather arduous and costly. Besides, significant efforts have to be spent
L65@P1: in order to develop schemes with spatial accuracy of order higher than second. An alternative constrained
L66@P1: transport method, based on the direct solution of the magnetic potential equation (thus avoiding staggered
L67@P1: grids), has been presented by [23].
L68@P1: In the present work we propose a new fully unsplit Godunov scheme for multidimensional MHD, based
L69@P1: on a combination of the Corner Transport Upwind of [8] and the mixed hyperbolic/parabolic divergence
L70@P1: cleaning technique of [12] (CTU-GLM). The proposed scheme has second order accuracy in both space
L71@P1: and time and adopts a cell-centered spatial collocation (no staggered mesh) of all flow variables, including
L72@P1: the magnetic field. The scheme is fully conservative in mass, momentum, magnetic induction and energy
L73@P1: and the divergence-free constraint is enforced via a mixed hyperbolic/parabolic correction which avoids the
L74@P1: computational cost associated with an elliptic cleaning deriving from a Hodge projection. A variant of the
L75@P1: scheme, which introduces divergence source terms breaking the conservative properties of some equations, is
L76@P1: also presented. We assess the accuracy and robustness of the scheme by a direct quantitative comparison with
L77@P1: the 8-wave formulation of [22] and the recently developed constrained transport method of [15, 16]. Other
L78@P1: similar implementations may be found in [14, 17]. The comparison is conveniently handled using the PLUTO
L79@P1: code for computational astrophysics [20] where both cell-centered and staggered-mesh implementations are
L80@P1: available.
L81@P1: Our motivating efforts are driven by issues of simplicity, efficiency and flexibility. In this sense, the
L82@P1: benefits offered by a method where all of the primary flow variables are discretized at the same spatial
L83@P1: location considerably ease the extension to adaptive grids, to more complex physics and to schemes with
L84@P1: higher than second order accuracy. The latter possibility will be explored in a companion paper.

L15: ### Abstract. The exact Riemann problem solutions of the usual equations of ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) can have negative pressures, if the initial data has $\nabla\cdot{\bf B}\ne 0$. This creates a problem for numerical solving because in a first order finite-volume conservative Godunov-type method one cannot avoid jumps in the normal magnetic field component even if the magnetic field was divergenceless in the three-dimensional sense.
L16: We show that by allowing magnetic monopoles in MHD equations and properly taking into account the magnetostatic contribution to the Lorentz force, an additional source term appears in Faraday's law only. Using the Harten-Lax-vanLeer-Einfeldt (HLL) Riemann solver and discretizing the source term in a specific manner, we obtain a method which is positive and conservative. We show positivity by extensive numerical experimentation.
L17: This MHD-HLL method is positive and conservative but rather diffusive, thus we show how to hybridize this method with the Roe method to obtain a much higher accuracy while still retaining positivity. The result is a fully robust positive conservative scheme for ideal MHD, whose accuracy and efficiency properties are similar to the first order Roe method and which keeps $\nabla\cdot{\bf B}$ small in the same sense as Powell's method.

L18@P0: Widespread applications of the ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations emerged in many disciplines,
L19@P0: including, but not limited to, astrophysical and magnetically confined fusion plasma applications. The
L20@P0: mentioned applications, usually deal with extreme conditions like near vacuum up to ultra-high density
L21@P0: environments where shocks of varying type and strength are the rule rather than the exception. Hence, the
L22@P0: accuracy and robustness of numerical simulation codes are very important.
L23@P0: Yet, the mathematical model of ideal MHD has some shortcomings that can cause the results to become
L24@P0: unphysical. As neither the full set of universally valid thermodynamics laws nor the divergence-free condition

L48@P1: methods with special focus on the hyperbolic divergence cleaning as we find it particularly useful in the
L49@P1: context of highly efficient, highly parallelizable numerical schemes for large-scale applications.
L50@P1: Another natural admissibility criterion is given by the universally valid laws of thermodynamics. Most
L51@P1: numerical schemes do not take the second law of thermodynamics directly into account but rather equip
L52@P1: the system with a minute amount of diffusion. We seek to derive a numerical scheme that complies with
L53@P1: the laws of thermodynamics and especially the second law, i.e. the entropy inequality. Following the work
L54@P1: of e.g. [2, 3, 4, 5], we use this law as an additional admissibility criterion to construct discretizations that
L55@P1: agree with the laws of thermodynamics. In this way, we enforce that the solution does not converge towards
L56@P1: physically irrelevant solutions which increases their numerical robustness, as thermodynamically impossible
L57@P1: physical processes that could e.g. lead to negative thermal pressures are forbidden.
L58@P1: In this work, we derive a new mathematical model that is built to explicitly take into account all the
L59@P1: mentioned relevant physics in order to impede unphysical results of numerical simulations. We start from
L60@P1: first principles to avoid commonly done simplifications that, as we explain herein, make the typically used
L61@P1: classic mathematical model of ideal MHD unsuitable in describing the behavior of physical flows in certain
L62@P1: regimes of numerically computed, discrete solutions.
L63@P1: For this, we derive a new system of equations, which we deem the ideal GLM-MHD equations, that
L64@P1: allows the construction of a novel magnetic field divergence diminishing scheme that naturally complies with
L65@P1: thermodynamics. Furthermore, we investigate our new model in great detail and present both the methods
L66@P1: we use as well as the details to allow a straightforward implementation of our scheme into the reader’s own
L67@P1: simulation code.
L68@P1: We shortly summarize the new contributions presented in this work:
L69@P1: • We derive the ideal MHD equations from the compressible Euler equations where we explicitly allow
L70@P1: non-zero magnetic field divergence in Maxwell’s equations. We physically motivate and highlight
L71@P1: important findings (Sec. 2)
L72@P1: • We derive a new physically motivated mathematical model, the ideal GLM-MHD equations which we
L73@P1: thoroughly investigate from both mathematical and physical perspectives (Sec. 3.4)
L74@P1: • We derive entropy stable numerical flux functions. We give all necessary details to code the high-order
L75@P1: scheme we are describing in a straightforward manner (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3)
L76@P1: 2. The ideal MHD equations in the case of ∇ · B 6= 0
L77@P1: We begin with the three-dimensional compressible Euler equations describing non-magnetized single-fluid
L78@P1: flows. We then couple the effect of magnetic fields to the model. We find that the classic model of ideal
L79@P1: MHD in the form of conservation laws is not valid for arbitrary flows, but only for fluids where (1.1) holds
L80@P1: exactly. Interestingly, our derivations reveal results that are known from previous publications [6, 7] while our
L81@P1: independent and fundamentally different approach motivates these findings with a solely physically motivated
L82@P1: mindset which eases the interpretation.
L83@P1: An important first step is, due to the findings of Brackbill and Barnes [1, eq. (2)], see also (1.2), that we
L84@P1: shouldn’t assume the divergence-free condition of the magnetic field (1.1) is fulfilled exactly at all times in
L85@P1: numerical simulations. In fact, Dirac [8] showed that quantum mechanics does not preclude the existence of
L86@P1: isolated magnetic monopoles although physicists often reason that magnetic monopoles are unlikely to exist.
L87@P1: Their reasoning mainly comes from the fact that quantum mechanics, as it is usually established, seems
L88@P1: possible only when there are no isolated magnetic monopoles. Dirac, however, disproved this view. One of the
L89@P1: most important theoretical motivations of introducing magnetic monopoles is to obtain Maxwell’s equations
L90@P1: in symmetric form with regard to charges. Note that the Maxwell equations retain all their properties, such
L91@P1-2: 2as invariance under a global duality transformation that mixes electric and magnetic fields [9], when magnetic
L92@P2: monopoles are included, whether or not they exist.

L410@P4: A remarkable outcome of the physically motivated derivation is that we obtain a set of equations which is
L411@P4: known to have a number of desirable properties lacking in the classical ideal MHD equations. The system
L412@P4: (2.16a-d) is not only symmetrizable [12] but also Galilean invariant [3, 7, 13]. The non-conservative terms
L413@P4: found on the right hand side were first mentioned by Godunov [6] who investigated whether the equations
L414@P4: of ideal MHD can be put into symmetric hyperbolic form. Interestingly, he found the same additional
L415@P4: non-conservative terms were required to obtain a PDE system that is symmetrizable, he took an altogether
L416@P4: different approach. The formulation of ideal MHD system considered here is often referred to as the eight-wave
L417@P4: formulation, because it supports eight traveling plane wave solutions. As the non-conservative term on the
L418@P4: right hand side is proportional to the divergence of the magnetic field, it is, on the continuous level, nothing
L419@P4: but adding zero in a clever way. Further advantages are that the flux Jacobian has only real eigenvalues and
L420@P4: the right eigenvectors are linearly independent, i.e. the ideal MHD equations in form (2.16a-d) are hyperbolic.
L421@P4: We will further investigate on the importance of these consequences later in this work.
L422@P4: Numerical simulations of this system are known to be more stable than the same numerical methods
L423@P4: applied to the original ideal MHD equations. This has been demonstrated by Powell [7] and numerically
L424@P4: confirmed by others (see e.g. [14, Sec. 6.1]). From the derivations allowing for ∇ · B 6= 0 a new physical
L425@P4: understanding for the addition of the non-conservative terms emerge and it is clear that their appearance are
L426@P4: essential parts of the system. We conclude that the classical ideal MHD equations are invalid for regions
L427@P4: where ∇ · B 6= 0 even if this deviation is only minor when the divergence of the magnetic field is controlled
L428@P4: to a sufficient degree. This is due to the fact that classical ideal MHD models contain the divergence-free
L429@P4: condition as a decoupled partial differential equation and hence assume that ∇ · B 6= 0 can never happen.

## Abstract

We describe a numerical algorithm based on Godunov methods for integrating the equations of compressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) in multidimensions. It combines a simple, dimensionally-unsplit integration method with the constrained transport (CT) discretization of the induction equation to enforce the divergence-free constraint. We present the results of a series of fully three-dimensional tests which indicate the method is second-order accurate for smooth solutions in all MHD wave families, and captures shocks, contact and rotational discontinuities well. However, it is also more diffusive than other more complex unsplit integrators combined with CT. Thus, the primary advantage of the method is its simplicity. It does not require a characteristic tracing step to construct interface values for the Riemann solver, it is straightforward to extend with additional physics, and it is suitable for use with nested and adaptive meshes. The method is implemented as one of two dimensionally unsplit MHD integrators in the Athena code, which is freely available for download from the web.

We adopt the most compact form of CT, which requires the field be represented by area-averages at cell faces. We demonstrate that the fluxes of the area-averaged field used by CT can be made consistent with the fluxes of the volume-averaged field returned by a Riemann solver if they obey certain simple relationships. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L15: ### Abstract. The exact Riemann problem solutions of the usual equations of ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) can have negative pressures, if the initial data has $\nabla\cdot{\bf B}\ne 0$. This creates a problem for numerical solving because in a first order finite-volume conservative Godunov-type method one cannot avoid jumps in the normal magnetic field component even if the magnetic field was divergenceless in the three-dimensional sense.
L16: We show that by allowing magnetic monopoles in MHD equations and properly taking into account the magnetostatic contribution to the Lorentz force, an additional source term appears in Faraday's law only. Using the Harten-Lax-vanLeer-Einfeldt (HLL) Riemann solver and discretizing the source term in a specific manner, we obtain a method which is positive and conservative. We show positivity by extensive numerical experimentation.
L17: This MHD-HLL method is positive and conservative but rather diffusive, thus we show how to hybridize this method with the Roe method to obtain a much higher accuracy while still retaining positivity. The result is a fully robust positive conservative scheme for ideal MHD, whose accuracy and efficiency properties are similar to the first order Roe method and which keeps $\nabla\cdot{\bf B}$ small in the same sense as Powell's method.
L18: As a special case, a method with similar characteristics for accuracy and robustness is obtained for the Euler equations as well.

L5@P0: Abstract
L6@P0: The paper presents two contributions in the context of the numerical simulation of magnetized fluid dynamics.
L7@P0: First, we show how to extend the ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations with an inbuilt magnetic
L8@P0: field divergence cleaning mechanism in such a way that the resulting model is consistent with the second
L9@P0: law of thermodynamics. As a byproduct of these derivations, we show that not all of the commonly used
L10@P0: divergence cleaning extensions of the ideal MHD equations are thermodynamically consistent. Secondly, we
L11@P0: present a numerical scheme obtained by constructing a specific finite volume discretization that is consistent
L12@P0: with the discrete thermodynamic entropy. It includes a mechanism to control the discrete divergence error
L13@P0: of the magnetic field by construction and is Galilean invariant. We implement the new high-order MHD
L14@P0: solver in the adaptive mesh refinement code FLASH where we compare the divergence cleaning efficiency to
L15@P0: the constrained transport solver available in FLASH (unsplit staggered mesh scheme).
L16@P0: Keywords: magnetohydrodynamics, entropy stability, divergence-free magnetic field, divergence cleaning
L17@P0: 1. Introduction
L18@P0: Widespread applications of the ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations emerged in many disciplines,
L19@P0: including, but not limited to, astrophysical and magnetically confined fusion plasma applications. The
L20@P0: mentioned applications, usually deal with extreme conditions like near vacuum up to ultra-high density
L21@P0: environments where shocks of varying type and strength are the rule rather than the exception. Hence, the
L22@P0: accuracy and robustness of numerical simulation codes are very important.
L23@P0: Yet, the mathematical model of ideal MHD has some shortcomings that can cause the results to become
L24@P0: unphysical. As neither the full set of universally valid thermodynamics laws nor the divergence-free condition
L25@P0: of the magnetic field is directly coupled into the classic mathematical model of ideal MHD, it is possible to
L26@P0: obtain physically invalid solutions.
L27@P0: In order to single out physically relevant solutions, we have to augment the system with additional
L28@P0: admissibility criteria. One admissibility criterion in the case of ideal MHD is the divergence-free condition of
L29@P0: the magnetic field that is expressed by Gauß’s law for magnetism
L30@P0: ∇ · B = 0. (1.1)
L31@P0: The implementation of (1.1) into a numerical approximation is a major difficulty. As detailed in the early
L32@P0: 1980s by Brackbill and Barnes [1, eq. (2)], numerical discretization errors always have a noticeable impact on
L33@P0: the temporal evolution of the magnetic field divergence:

L50@P1: Another natural admissibility criterion is given by the universally valid laws of thermodynamics. Most
L51@P1: numerical schemes do not take the second law of thermodynamics directly into account but rather equip
L52@P1: the system with a minute amount of diffusion. We seek to derive a numerical scheme that complies with
L53@P1: the laws of thermodynamics and especially the second law, i.e. the entropy inequality. Following the work
L54@P1: of e.g. [2, 3, 4, 5], we use this law as an additional admissibility criterion to construct discretizations that
L55@P1: agree with the laws of thermodynamics. In this way, we enforce that the solution does not converge towards
L56@P1: physically irrelevant solutions which increases their numerical robustness, as thermodynamically impossible
L57@P1: physical processes that could e.g. lead to negative thermal pressures are forbidden.
L58@P1: In this work, we derive a new mathematical model that is built to explicitly take into account all the
L59@P1: mentioned relevant physics in order to impede unphysical results of numerical simulations. We start from
L60@P1: first principles to avoid commonly done simplifications that, as we explain herein, make the typically used
L61@P1: classic mathematical model of ideal MHD unsuitable in describing the behavior of physical flows in certain
L62@P1: regimes of numerically computed, discrete solutions.
L63@P1: For this, we derive a new system of equations, which we deem the ideal GLM-MHD equations, that
L64@P1: allows the construction of a novel magnetic field divergence diminishing scheme that naturally complies with
L65@P1: thermodynamics. Furthermore, we investigate our new model in great detail and present both the methods
L66@P1: we use as well as the details to allow a straightforward implementation of our scheme into the reader’s own
L67@P1: simulation code.
L68@P1: We shortly summarize the new contributions presented in this work:
L69@P1: • We derive the ideal MHD equations from the compressible Euler equations where we explicitly allow
L70@P1: non-zero magnetic field divergence in Maxwell’s equations. We physically motivate and highlight
L71@P1: important findings (Sec. 2)
L72@P1: • We derive a new physically motivated mathematical model, the ideal GLM-MHD equations which we
L73@P1: thoroughly investigate from both mathematical and physical perspectives (Sec. 3.4)
L74@P1: • We derive entropy stable numerical flux functions. We give all necessary details to code the high-order
L75@P1: scheme we are describing in a straightforward manner (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3)
L76@P1: 2. The ideal MHD equations in the case of ∇ · B 6= 0
L77@P1: We begin with the three-dimensional compressible Euler equations describing non-magnetized single-fluid
L78@P1: flows. We then couple the effect of magnetic fields to the model. We find that the classic model of ideal
L79@P1: MHD in the form of conservation laws is not valid for arbitrary flows, but only for fluids where (1.1) holds
L80@P1: exactly. Interestingly, our derivations reveal results that are known from previous publications [6, 7] while our
L81@P1: independent and fundamentally different approach motivates these findings with a solely physically motivated
L82@P1: mindset which eases the interpretation.
L83@P1: An important first step is, due to the findings of Brackbill and Barnes [1, eq. (2)], see also (1.2), that we
L84@P1: shouldn’t assume the divergence-free condition of the magnetic field (1.1) is fulfilled exactly at all times in
L85@P1: numerical simulations. In fact, Dirac [8] showed that quantum mechanics does not preclude the existence of
L86@P1: isolated magnetic monopoles although physicists often reason that magnetic monopoles are unlikely to exist.
L87@P1: Their reasoning mainly comes from the fact that quantum mechanics, as it is usually established, seems
L88@P1: possible only when there are no isolated magnetic monopoles. Dirac, however, disproved this view. One of the
L89@P1: most important theoretical motivations of introducing magnetic monopoles is to obtain Maxwell’s equations
L90@P1: in symmetric form with regard to charges. Note that the Maxwell equations retain all their properties, such
L91@P1-2: 2as invariance under a global duality transformation that mixes electric and magnetic fields [9], when magnetic
L92@P2: monopoles are included, whether or not they exist.
L93@P2: During the derivation of the classic ideal MHD equations in conservative form, (1.1) is used to simplify
L94@P2: the computations. However, this ultimately destroys the validity of the system of ideal MHD equations for
L95@P2: flows where the divergence-free condition is not fulfilled to a certain extent, which is generally the case in
L96@P2: discrete approximations. This is commonly found in simulations due to errors caused by any given numerical
L97@P2: approximation. Note that this more general form of the ideal MHD equations is, of course, perfectly valid in
L98@P2: the case of ∇ · B = 0, as the only difference is that certain terms aren’t neglected early on in the derivation.
